what_it_means_paragraphs: A Level 2 EV charger needs a dedicated 240-volt circuit pulled from your electrical panel to wherever the car parks — garage, driveway, carport, side of the house. The circuit is 40 or 50 amps in most residential installs, and it's a continuous load, which means the breaker, the wire, and the panel all have to be sized for sustained draw, not just the brief peak you see on a clothes dryer.

"Installation" covers the load calculation on your existing panel, the new breaker, the conduit and wire run, the hardwire termination (or the NEMA 14-50 outlet if you're using a plug-in unit), the charger mount, the connection to your home Wi-Fi if the unit is smart, and the permit and inspection. None of this is a single-trip job — it's a planned electrical install with code requirements.

why_city_closing_note_template: If your home matches one of these patterns, the load calculation is what tells you whether you need a full service upgrade, a sub-panel, or just a breaker swap. We'd rather quote you the smaller job when the smaller job is the right answer.

scenario_cards.title: 1950s-1970s split-levels & ranches
scenario_cards.body: Most are on 100-amp service. The garage panel run is usually the cleanest path. The constraint is panel capacity — a 100-amp panel feeding the rest of the house often can't fit a continuous 40-amp EV draw.
scenario_cards.typical_install: Panel upgrade plus 48-amp hardwired Wall Connector, or NEMA 14-50 on a 40-amp circuit if the load calc fits.

scenario_cards.title: 1970s-1990s colonials & traditionals
scenario_cards.body: 200-amp service in most cases. The garage is often detached or under-house with a long run from the basement panel. Many of these homes already have a sub-panel in the garage — that simplifies the install dramatically.
scenario_cards.typical_install: 50-amp circuit, hardwired Tesla Wall Connector or ChargePoint Home Flex, conduit run from basement panel or existing garage sub-panel.

scenario_cards.title: 2000s-2020s townhomes & newer detached
scenario_cards.body: 200-amp or 225-amp panels, garage right next to the panel, plenty of capacity. The cleanest installs we do — wire pull is under 10 feet, charger mount is on a finished wall, and the conduit is mostly invisible.
scenario_cards.typical_install: 48-amp hardwired Wall Connector or smart charger, clean conduit run, finished in 3-4 hours.

problem_cards.title: Tesla Wall Connector — hardwired, 48 amps
problem_cards.body: The default install for new Tesla owners. Hardwired at 48 amps for the fastest residential charging speed. We mount the unit, run the circuit from your panel, terminate, commission, and pair to your Tesla account. Typical job: 3-4 hours.

problem_cards.title: NEMA 14-50 outlet for portable Level 2
problem_cards.body: The flexible option. Same outlet that an RV uses. Lets you plug in the portable Level 2 cord that came with your car (most makes ship one). Cheaper than hardwired and lets you take the cord on road trips.

problem_cards.title: ChargePoint Home Flex install
problem_cards.body: Smart charger with app control, hardwired up to 50 amps or plug-in at 40 amps. Popular with Ford Lightning, Rivian, and Mustang Mach-E owners who want load-sharing and remote monitoring.

problem_cards.title: JuiceBox / Wallbox Pulsar Plus install
problem_cards.body: Smart chargers with utility-program integration (some support {utility_provider}'s EV time-of-use rates). Hardwired or plug-in. We install the electrical side; you configure the app.

problem_cards.title: Two-charger install (two-EV households)
problem_cards.body: Two chargers can share a feeder if the equipment supports load sharing.

problem_cards.title: Outdoor / driveway install with weather-rated equipment
problem_cards.body: For carports, driveway pedestals, or detached garages. Requires weather-rated charger and conduit.

problem_cards.title: Charger plus panel upgrade — combo project
problem_cards.body: When the load calculation says the existing panel can't fit the EV load. We do both in the same project.

problem_cards.title: Service-entrance or feeder repair for an existing EV install
problem_cards.body: If your current charger throttles, trips a breaker, or warms the outlet, the cause is almost always upstream.

process_steps.title: Phone consult — car, charger, panel
process_steps.body: {owner_name} or someone from his team picks up. We ask three things: what car (or cars) you have, whether you've picked a charger yet, and where the panel is relative to where the car parks.

process_steps.title: On-site load calc and written estimate
process_steps.body: We come to your house, open the panel, look at the route from panel to charger location, and run a load calculation. You get a written estimate before the project is scheduled.

process_steps.title: Permit pulled with {county}
process_steps.body: EV charger installs at residential amperages require a permit. We file it. Typically takes 2-5 business days. Permit fee is included in the estimate.

process_steps.title: Install day — 3-5 hours typical
process_steps.body: Install the dedicated breaker. Run the conduit from panel to charger location. Pull the wire. Mount the charger or the NEMA 14-50 outlet. Terminate at both ends. Test, energize, verify charging.

process_steps.title: Inspection by {county}
process_steps.body: The county inspector comes out within the scheduled window. We meet them on-site and pull the permit closed. You get a copy of the signed inspection card.

process_steps.title: A clean exit, with documentation
process_steps.body: When we leave, you have a working charger, a copy of the permit, a copy of the inspection card, and a written workmanship warranty.

pricing_intro_template: We publish our prices because we'd want them published if we were hiring an electrician. Most {city_name} electricians won't quote a number until they've been on-site. Ours:

pricing_items.label: Hardwired Level 2 charger install (40-50 amp)
pricing_items.detail: Covers permit, dedicated breaker, conduit + wire run (typical 15-30 feet from panel to charger), hardwire termination, charger mount, and inspection coordination.

pricing_items.label: NEMA 14-50 outlet install
pricing_items.detail: Covers permit, breaker, conduit + wire, outlet box, GFCI/EVSE breaker, and inspection. Cheaper than hardwired because no charger mounting is required.

pricing_items.label: Outdoor / driveway install
pricing_items.detail: Weather-rated conduit, longer wire pull, pedestal mount or wall mount on exterior surface.

pricing_items.label: Charger plus panel upgrade combo
pricing_items.detail: When the load calc says you need both. Single permit covers both jobs. One day of work instead of two visits.

pricing_items.label: Two-charger install
pricing_items.detail: Two dedicated circuits if panel capacity allows, or shared-feeder install with load-sharing equipment.

pricing_items.label: Permits & inspection
pricing_items.detail: No surprise add-ons at the end.

faq_items.question: How much does Level 2 EV charger installation cost in {city_name_with_state}?
faq_items.answer_html: A hardwired Level 2 charger install (40-50 amp circuit) in {city_name} runs $1,500 to $2,500, including permit, dedicated breaker, conduit and wire, hardwire termination, charger mount, and inspection. A NEMA 14-50 outlet for a portable Level 2 cord runs $800-$1,500. Outdoor or driveway installs add $300-$600. If a panel upgrade is needed alongside the charger, the combo runs $4,000-$6,500.

faq_items.question: NEMA 14-50 outlet vs. hardwired — which should I get?
faq_items.answer_html: A NEMA 14-50 outlet is cheaper and more flexible — you plug in the portable Level 2 cord that came with your car. Hardwired is faster (no plug-load 80% derating, so a Tesla Wall Connector hits the full 48 amps), looks cleaner, and is the only option for some chargers in their fastest mode. We recommend based on your car, charger choice, and how often you would swap setups.

faq_items.question: Do I need a panel upgrade for my EV charger?
faq_items.answer_html: Sometimes. A 200-amp panel feeding a normal {city_name} home usually fits a 40 or 50-amp EV circuit without an upgrade. A 100-amp panel feeding a modern home (central AC, electric water heater, range, dryer) often cannot — the load calculation comes out over the safe limit. We do the calc on-site and tell you up front. If an upgrade is needed, we handle both jobs in the same project.

We give the time window with the written estimate.
